::: {.callout-note title="What this page is"}
A recipe for linking a child to its parents, and from there to siblings or to a
parent's characteristics. It is the first step of a [sibling
design](special-designs.qmd#sibling-designs), and also of any
study that needs the mother's or father's education, income or diagnoses.
:::

## What the link is {#what-the-link-is}

BEF has two columns for the link: `mor_id` and `far_id`, the person id of the
mother and of the father. They come from the Civil Registration System (CPR).
Three things about them are easy to miss.

**They are the legal parents, not necessarily the biological ones.** CPR holds
the legal relationship, and it keeps only the current one: "Danish legislation
prohibits the CRS of keeping information on previous legal relationships. Thus,
for example, for adopted children, the CRS contains information on the legal
parents only" (Pedersen et al. 2006). Statistics Denmark (DST) is more careful
still: "Parent child relations in CPR is an administrative relations, which
cannot necessarily be sided be legal or biological parent-child relations"
(DST, documentation of the *Relatives* statistics, accuracy and reliability).

**A missing id means no link is registered.** It does not mean the parent is
unknown to the family. See the coverage table below.

**A parent can be of the other sex than the column.** A co-mother is registered
in the father's place, and DST marks that in FTBARN (see [Adoption and other
non-biological relations](#adoption)).

## Coverage by birth cohort {#coverage}

CPR started in 1968, and the parental links were first built from families
living at the same address. Until 1978 a link was erased when the child moved
away from home, when a parent moved, when the child had children or when the
child turned 18. From 1978 links are kept permanently, and from then on they
follow the legal relationship (Pedersen et al. 2006).

  | Born in Denmark | What DST and the CPR papers say                                                              |
  | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | 1950            | 8.0% have a link to a mother (Pedersen et al. 2006)                                          |
  | 1960            | 98.7% have a link to a mother. All persons born in 1960 or later have a complete link to both parents in the Family Relations Database (Pedersen 2013) |
  | 1960-1968       | The links are "almost correct" (Pedersen et al. 2006)                                        |
  | 1969 or later   | The links are considered 100% correct (Pedersen et al. 2006; Pedersen 2013)                  |
  | 1970            | 99.9% have a link to a mother (Pedersen et al. 2006)                                         |

For people **born abroad** the links are much rarer, because parent and child are
not linked at immigration, and a parent needs a Danish CPR number to be linked at
all (Pedersen et al. 2006; DST, *Relatives*, accuracy and reliability). In
Pedersen et al., 29.8% of those born abroad in 1980 and 94.2% of those born in
1990 have a mother link. Expect a missing `mor_id` and `far_id` for most
immigrants, and report the share.

For **newborns**, the second parent can be missing for up to half a year after
the birth, because it takes that long to register. DST names this as most
common for births in the second half of a year and for unmarried parents, and
advises against studying the relatives of newborns in the latest reference
year (DST, *Relatives*, accuracy and reliability).

Persons born before 1967 have too few registered parents and siblings, and for
those born before 1935 the undercount may be very large (DST, *Relatives*,
accuracy and reliability).

## Step 1 - Take the link from BEF {#step-1}

BEF is a snapshot register (see [DST pitfalls](dst-pitfalls.qmd), pitfall 5), so
the same child has one row per snapshot, and `mor_id` and `far_id` can differ
between snapshots or be missing in some of them. A parent can be added to the
child after the first snapshots, for example. There is no single correct value,
so you have to pick a rule and write it in your methods.

The rule below takes, for each child, the first non-missing value from the
snapshots at or after the child's birth. For a child born before the first BEF
snapshot (December 1985) that is the link as it stood in 1985 or later.

```r
# Step 1: one mother and one father per child, from BEF ------------------------
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr)   # the verbs are translated to SQL and run in DuckDB

# cohort_pnrs: the pnr of the children you want parents for (your cohort)
bef <- read_register("bef") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE)
# Columns: pnr | foed_dag | mor_id | far_id | referencetid

# The first non-missing mother id in a snapshot at or after birth. Check how a
# missing id looks in your delivery (NA or an empty string) before relying on
# is.na().
mother <- bef %>%
  filter(referencetid >= foed_dag, !is.na(mor_id)) %>%
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  slice_min(referencetid, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(pnr, foed_dag, mor_id)

father <- bef %>%
  filter(referencetid >= foed_dag, !is.na(far_id)) %>%
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  slice_min(referencetid, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(pnr, far_id)

# full_join: a child with only one registered parent keeps its row, with NA
# for the other
parents <- mother %>%
  full_join(father, by = "pnr") %>%
  collect()
```

A child with `NA` for both has no link in BEF. Count them by birth year before
you go on, and report how many children each analysis loses on that account. A
different rule, such as the most frequent value or the latest snapshot, is
equally valid if you state it. What matters is that the rule is the same for
every child.

## Step 2 - Siblings {#siblings}

Siblings are children with the same parent id, and the type depends on how many
parents they share:

- **Full siblings** share both mother and father.
- **Maternal half-siblings** share the mother only, and **paternal
  half-siblings** share the father only.

Do not count a pair as full siblings when one of the fathers is missing. The
pair shares a mother, so it is at least a maternal half-sibling pair, and the
father is unknown. Say in your methods how you handle those pairs, and run the
analysis both ways if there are many of them.

The siblings you need are not only the ones in your cohort. If the exposed
child has a brother who is not in the cohort, he is still a sibling, so build
`parents` above for everyone whose mother or father is in your cohort, not only
for the cohort itself.

```r
# Step 2: sibling pairs and their type ----------------------------------------
pairs_by <- function(key) {
  a <- parents %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_a"))
  b <- parents %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_b"))
  by <- setNames(paste0(key, "_b"), paste0(key, "_a"))
  a %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[paste0(key, "_a")]])) %>%
    inner_join(b, by = by, keep = TRUE) %>%   # keep = TRUE: both id columns stay
    filter(pnr_a < pnr_b)
}

sibling_pairs <- bind_rows(pairs_by("mor_id"), pairs_by("far_id")) %>%
  mutate(
    same_mother = coalesce(mor_id_a == mor_id_b, FALSE),
    same_father = coalesce(far_id_a == far_id_b, FALSE),
    type = case_when(
      same_mother & same_father ~ "full",
      same_mother               ~ "maternal half",
      same_father               ~ "paternal half"
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(pnr_a, pnr_b, type)
```

The `famnet` package does the same job with `fmn_siblings()` and gives the
relationship type directly. See [Algorithms and
packages](packages-overview.qmd).

For a sibling analysis you also need a family id for the strata. For full siblings the
mother and father ids together identify the family. With half-siblings in the data, a person can belong to
more than one family, so decide how the strata are formed and state it.

## Step 3 - A parent's characteristic at the child's birth {#parent-characteristics}

Use `mor_id` or `far_id` as the `pnr` of the parent, and look the parent up in
the register that holds the characteristic, in the year that matters. That
could be the mother's education, income or employment at the child's birth, or
her diagnoses before it. The year rule is the one for any other person, so it
is not repeated here. See [When each dimension is
measured](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#timing) for education, employment and
income.

Before you do this, check that the parent ids match the person ids in the
registers you look them up in. Most non-missing `mor_id` values should appear
as a `pnr` in BEF. If they do not, the ids are not comparable in your project
and the lookup will return nothing.

A parent who was not living in Denmark in the year, or who died before it,
will have no row. That is a missing value in your analysis, so handle it as one
(see [Missing data](missing-data.qmd)).

## Adoption and other non-biological relations {#adoption}

BEF only has the current legal parents, so it cannot tell you whether the
relation is adoptive. FTBARN, the child file of the fertility database, can.
It has one row per child from 1973 and, besides the parents (`mor1`, `far1`),
two columns that mark the relation: `mor_foed_adop` for the mother and
`far_foed_adop` for the father.

DST describes them as marking whether information in the background registers
(the Adoption Register, CPR and the Medical Birth Register) points to an
adoptive or other non-biological relation. Codes 11 to 18 are a presumed
non-biological relation, codes 21 to 23 a presumed biological one, and 30 to 39
cover children born abroad, children born before 1973 and relations with no
sign of adoption or early registration. For the father's column DST's text gives
1991 instead of 1973 in the grouping, so the cut-off for fathers is unclear. The full list is in
the [value sets under FTBARN](register-reference.qmd#ftbarn).

Four points from DST's own documentation:

- **It is presumed, not known.** DST: "A biological relation can only be
  determined with a DNA test, which is not available in the background
  registers." A child conceived with donor sperm or donor egg looks like a
  biological relation in the registers.
- **Do not count adoptions with it.** DST: "It makes no sense to count the
  number of adopted or biological relations from the variable." Use it to
  select or exclude, not to estimate how many.
- **Code 14 is not an adoption.** It marks a parent of the other sex than the
  column, so a co-mother is registered in the father's column with code 14.
- **Code 12 can concern the other parent.** The child is in the Adoption
  Register, but the adoptive relation may be to the other parent.

In FTBARN, `mor1` is the first mother valid in CPR, and `mor2` the latest one
when it differs. The relation of `mor1` to the child is in `mor_foed_adop`.

DST changed the adoption columns in a correction of 30 October 2025. Version 2
of the fertility tables for reference years up to 2023 sets
`mor_foed_adop` and `far_foed_adop` to unknown (99) for 2019 to 2023, because
data are missing to form new adoption markers for those years. Version 1 held
other values by mistake. For children born in 2019 to 2023 adoption therefore
cannot be identified in FTBARN, and a delivery made before the correction has
wrong values for those years (DST, FTBARN register history). Check the `version`
column in your delivery.

```r
# Adoption markers for the cohort (FTBARN) --------------------------------------
ftbarn <- read_register("ftbarn") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  select(pnr, mor1, far1, mor_foed_adop, far_foed_adop) %>%
  collect()

# Presumed biological mother and father: DST's codes 21 to 23
ftbarn <- ftbarn %>%
  mutate(
    mother_presumed_bio = as.integer(mor_foed_adop) %in% 21:23,
    father_presumed_bio = as.integer(far_foed_adop) %in% 21:23
  )
```

State in your methods that the group is *presumed* biological. A child with
code 31 to 39 is not non-biological. It is a child the registers cannot say
anything about.

## What to write in your methods {#methods}

- The source of the link (BEF `mor_id` and `far_id`, and FTBARN if you use it)
  and the rule for choosing between snapshots.
- That the link is the legal, administrative relation in CPR.
- The birth cohorts you include and the share with a missing parent link, by
  birth year, and how immigrants were handled.
- How half-siblings and pairs with a missing parent were handled.
- If you use the adoption markers, which codes you used and that the relation
  is presumed.
